title: Washington Resigns His Commission
text:
By late 1783 the War of Independence was over and the last British troops had left New York. George Washington was the most admired man in the new United States, and he commanded the only national army. Many people at home and abroad assumed he would use that position to rule.

Instead he rode to Annapolis, Maryland, where the Continental Congress was then meeting. On December 23, 1783, he appeared before Congress in the Maryland State House. In a short speech he thanked his officers and the army, commended the country to God, and announced that he was retiring from public life. He then handed his commission, the document that had made him commander in chief in 1775, back to the president of Congress, Thomas Mifflin.

The journals of Congress record the ceremony. Witnesses described members and spectators in tears. Washington left the same day and reached his home at Mount Vernon on Christmas Eve.

His return to private life helped establish the principle that the army is subordinate to civilian government. He came back to public life only years later, through election.
lesson: Handing power back when you could keep it is one of the strongest ways to prove you deserved it. People trust the leader who is willing to leave.
source: Journals of the Continental Congress, December 23, 1783; Washington's address to Congress on resigning his commission
